# DevSecOps with coding agents at Papaya

## Scope and evidence

**Source:** [DevSecOps Challenge 1 — DevSecOps with Coding Agents at Papaya](https://github.com/papaya-insurtech/pumpkin/blob/main/Hiring/DevSecOps_Challenges/DevSecOps_Challenge_1.md), including Appendix A. This is a proposed target operating model, not an assessment of Papaya's actual controls. I have no access to its systems, code, contracts, or production data. No control below is claimed to exist or to establish certification or legal compliance.

**Explicit challenge requirements:** use a coding agent; design a framework and workflow for agent-assisted DevSecOps against the stated platform and opposing engineering/compliance positions; submit deliverables and *complete, raw, unedited* conversations from every agent session in one GitHub repository. The prompt leaves deliverable format open. It does not require deployment or proof of existing compliance.

**Working assumptions to validate:** Papaya can separate production from non-production identities and isolate production deployment credentials; a central identity provider can supply named human accounts with multi-factor authentication; GitHub branch protection, environments and workload federation are available under the organization's plan; infrastructure definitions and service deployment workflows can be brought under review; each partner's residency, retention, disclosure and breach-notification requirements must be mapped with counsel and partner owners. Where a platform cannot enforce a gate, block that deployment path until an equivalent control exists rather than treating a written policy as enforcement.

**Decision:** agents may diagnose and propose changes, but are never production approvers or holders of production write credentials. A named, independent human reviews the specific revision and production plan; a separately gated deployment identity applies only that revision. Engineering keeps a fast path to read-only diagnostics and staging. Compliance gets a technical boundary on production writes. A click alone is insufficient: authorization, artifact identity, isolation, audit and rollback must also hold.

## Trust boundaries and enforcement

| Boundary | Proposed enforcement | Failure behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Engineer laptop and agent | Remove standing production write roles from human single sign-on profiles; provide time-limited, named, scoped read-only diagnostic access through approved access paths, with logs and sensitive-field redaction. Agent tools inherit no broader rights than the process. Put production write behind organization/account/project identity controls, not prompts, shell aliases, repository instructions or an agent's self-report. | A laptop with prompts disabled can still edit local code, but cannot mutate production. Block or expire diagnostic access if identity or device requirements fail. |
| Agent extensions and data | Maintain a reviewed, version-pinned allowlist for Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and plugins; assess code, dependencies, tool permissions, network destinations and update provenance in an isolated test environment. Default deny unreviewed extensions for work involving company code or data; enforce on managed endpoints and controlled runner images, not just in agent configuration. Treat partner documents, logs, issue text, repository files and tool outputs as untrusted instructions. | An unreviewed server/plugin gets no company data or credentials. A prompt-injected document cannot authorize a tool or workflow. |
| Source and review | Protect default and production branches: required status checks, up-to-date reviewed changes, no direct pushes, no force push or routine administrator bypass, CODEOWNERS for infrastructure/security paths, independently named human reviewer(s), and stale-review dismissal on new commits. Protect workflow, CODEOWNERS and policy files with security-owned review. Restrict bot permissions; an agent identity cannot count as a human approver. | No merge if a review, check or protected-file ownership gate fails. Audit exceptional administrative bypass separately and investigate it. |
| Continuous integration and deployment | Separate untrusted pull-request checks from trusted planning and deployment workflows. Run pull-request jobs with read-only repository token, no cloud secrets, and isolated runners; never run untrusted pull-request code in a privileged `pull_request_target` or equivalent context. A protected-revision planning job may obtain a separate short-lived, production **read-only** identity. A production deployment job obtains a distinct short-lived **write** identity only after its protected-environment approval. Use GitHub OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation with trust restricted to the appropriate repository, branch, workflow/environment and audience; remove long-lived repository AWS keys and GitHub personal access tokens after replacing their use. Pin third-party actions to reviewed immutable references. | A pull request cannot obtain production credentials. A write job cannot assume a role if claims, audience, repository, ref or environment do not match. |
| Production approval and cloud authority | Configure a protected production environment with required named reviewers and self-review prevention; only the trusted deployment workflow may request its credential. Bind deployment to the reviewed commit, immutable build artifact digest, tenant/region and plan hash. Give the deploy principal least-privilege, scoped production write permissions; deny routine human/agent write paths at the AWS organization/account and Google Cloud organization/project identity boundaries where feasible, with monitored exception roles. Restrict k0s administration and Firebase release authority to controlled deploy identities. | No direct laptop apply, missing approval or changed plan can deploy. Emergency identity is separate, short-lived, logged, independently approved before use and reviewed again afterward. |

These gates need an adversarial test: attempt a direct laptop production write, a pull-request job credential request, an altered workflow, a self-approval, a commit pushed after approval, and a changed infrastructure plan. Each must fail at the relevant control plane. GitHub configuration alone does not stop a separately privileged cloud user; cloud identity and organization restrictions must close that route. Likewise, an OIDC role trust policy alone does not make a compromised runner harmless: keep runners ephemeral/isolated, scope roles tightly, and monitor their sessions. Configuration drift, cloud consoles, k0s credentials and Firebase release tokens are parallel write paths that must be inventoried and closed or documented as explicitly governed exceptions.

## Normal production change: end-to-end

1. **Request and classify.** Open a Linear change record with business owner, service, partner/country/region, data classification, intended behavior, risk, maintenance window, test and rollback owners. Check contractual residency and partner notification requirements; do not include medical records, identifiers, bank data or secrets in tickets, prompts, pull requests or build logs. Define success and abort signals before work starts.
2. **Develop and diagnose.** The engineer uses the coding agent against synthetic/redacted fixtures, staging, and scoped production read-only telemetry when needed. Repository and tool outputs are data, not instructions. If the agent asks to run a production write or use an unknown MCP server/plugin, stop that route; permission prompts may be off, so the cloud and network boundaries must still deny it. Record material agent-assisted changes in the pull request for reviewer context, without assuming the agent is an approver.
3. **Pull request.** Link the Linear record; provide architecture impact, partner/region scope, migration and backward-compatibility notes, threat considerations, test evidence, proposed infrastructure diff, rollout schedule, monitoring and rollback. Require separate human review by the relevant service owner and, for production identity, data-boundary or infrastructure changes, the security/platform owner. The author and agent cannot satisfy independent approval. Escalate high-risk cross-border or sensitive-data changes to the appropriate privacy/partner owner before deployment.
4. **Untrusted checks.** In isolated pull-request continuous integration, run relevant TypeScript/Node.js and Python tests, lint/type checks, migration tests, offline infrastructure validation/preview, secret scanning, dependency/container/image scanning, infrastructure-as-code policy checks and targeted security tests. Block on defined severity thresholds or require a time-bound, named exception with compensating controls; never silently waive findings. Validate Pulumi policy constraints and Serverless Framework package/configuration; test GraphQL authorization and tenancy boundaries when touched. Tests use synthetic data and no production credentials. Publish artifacts and findings with restricted visibility and redacted logs.
5. **Plan and independently review.** Before merge, reviewers inspect the pull-request source diff, offline preview and test evidence; approval binds to the reviewed commit. After merge, a protected-revision workflow, not pull-request code, generates the authoritative production preview using a separate short-lived, read-only planning identity for each affected scope (AWS, Google Cloud, k0s, Firebase). The preview identifies resource creates/updates/deletes, identity and data-access effects, tenant/region and cost/availability implications; a Pulumi plan alone does not cover Serverless packages or every Kubernetes/Firebase release, so attach their concrete release diffs and immutable digests too. A named independent production reviewer checks this exact plan against the merged source and request, explicitly flags destructive or cross-region changes, and approves the plan digest at the deployment gate. Limit preview access to authorized reviewers; do not put sensitive outputs in public pull-request comments. If the platform cannot produce a safe read-only production plan, use a separately reviewed equivalent and record the blind spots before approval.
6. **Gate and deploy.** Merge only after required pull-request checks and reviews. Build once from the protected revision, attest/store an immutable digest, and deploy that digest, not a mutable tag or a rebuilt artifact. For production, require a fresh protected-environment approval by a named human other than the initiator, **after** the authoritative plan is available. Present its digest and exact operations in the deployment run summary; capture the reviewer's named approval of that digest in a protected change record tied to the run, and make the trusted deploy job verify that record and the GitHub environment approval through authorized APIs rather than trusting an unchecked comment or a generic click. Record change ID, commit, artifact digest, approved plan digest, approver and deployment run. Before assuming its write role, the trusted workflow checks those values against the protected revision and approved artifact. Serialize conflicting changes per service/region; revalidate actual state before apply and stop for fresh independent review/approval if drift or an effective-plan change alters the approved operations. The write role is OIDC-federated only after the environment gate and is separate from the planning identity; a narrowly scoped trusted reconciliation job may use the read-only identity to check drift. If the tooling cannot apply exactly the reviewed operations, do not claim plan binding: block on any meaningful difference and require another approval. Use phased rollout/canary where supported, starting with an appropriate low-risk slice, never mixing partner datasets or regions for convenience. The pipeline, not the agent or engineer laptop, performs the production write.
7. **Observe and close.** Compare pre/post error rate, latency, queue depth, claim-processing accuracy, tenant-isolation signals and security/audit anomalies for a stated observation window. Assign a named primary and backup on-call owner with paging and escalation; consolidate AWS CloudWatch, Google Cloud and k0s/Firebase signals into a common incident view with tenant/region labels and traceable change IDs. Record deployment outcome and follow-up in Linear. If the threshold is exceeded, halt progression and roll back or forward-fix under the same approval rules; notify partner/privacy contacts when contractual or regulatory triggers apply.

**Rollback is a plan, not a button.** Preserve the previous immutable service artifact and infrastructure state/preview, rehearse reversal in staging, and define who authorizes it. Reverse deployment for stateless code; for Aurora PostgreSQL schema/data changes prefer expand-contract and a tested forward repair or restore decision because rolling back code cannot reverse destructive data migrations. For S3 documents and insurer data, verify backup, retention and restoration boundaries per tenant/region. Confirm recovery-point/recovery-time objectives with service owners; do not invent guarantees. Record who triggered rollback, what changed, and whether data integrity was verified.

### Example: production S3 claim-document access change

A claim-service engineer proposes restricting a production S3 document bucket policy for one insurer in Vietnam. The agent helps reproduce an authorization failure against synthetic objects and drafts a Pulumi change in a pull request. The engineer includes a read-only inventory of affected principals, before/after policy diff, least-privilege access tests, expected region and partner scope, and a rollback policy version. Security and service owners independently inspect the resource preview for accidental public access, cross-tenant grants or denied legitimate claim processing; required checks pass. A named independent production approver approves the exact revision and plan. The gated pipeline assumes its short-lived AWS role, rechecks drift, applies the approved change, then observes AccessDenied rates, claim processing, audit events and S3 access patterns. If legitimate partner access breaks, the on-call owner halts rollout and restores the previously reviewed policy through the controlled path; if an active exposure requires immediate containment, use the emergency path below. A code or policy rollback does not automatically recover data already disclosed; start the incident process for that risk.

## Emergency production change

Example: audit signals show an insurer's claim documents may be readable by another tenant. On-call declares an incident and creates an incident/change ID; the incident commander identifies the affected region, bucket/principals and first containment action. A **named, independent human** reviews the exact emergency action, scope and expected impact and approves it before any production write; the primary or backup on-call approver is paged immediately. Prefer the pre-tested, narrowly scoped containment runbook through the gated pipeline (for example deny the suspect principal while preserving evidence); prior approval of the runbook is not a substitute for reviewing this incident's specific action. If the pipeline is unavailable, the reviewer approves an incident-bound just-in-time emergency-role activation for a different named operator, with multi-factor authentication, short expiry and the smallest write scope. Record both identities, the reviewed action and approval before activation; monitor the operator's session and compare executed commands against that scope. Never let an agent activate or approve this role. If no independent approver is reachable, escalate to the backup/incident commander; do not perform an unreviewed production write and document the resulting exposure and delay. Preserve evidence, test that access is contained without spreading sensitive data, monitor service impact, and engage security, privacy, the partner owner and legal to decide notification obligations by jurisdiction and contract. Reconcile any console/hotfix change back into Pulumi or other version-controlled desired state, revoke the emergency grant, independently review the diff and incident timeline, and rehearse recovery. Emergency access shortens the route to review; it does not waive named pre-change approval.

## Data, audit and operations

Maintain a per-partner/country data-flow inventory for AWS S3/Aurora, Google Cloud Vertex AI/Gemini, k0s workloads, Firebase Hosting and external model endpoints. Map where content, prompts, embeddings, logs, backups and inference are processed and retained; enforce tenant separation in identity, storage access, application authorization and tests. Decide permitted model endpoints and transfers with privacy/legal and each partner; use minimum necessary fields, redaction/tokenization, encryption in transit and at rest, access logging and retention/deletion schedules. Do not send live medical documents, national IDs, bank accounts or production secrets to an agent or third-party MCP server merely to debug faster. For production AI agents consuming uploaded documents, isolate tools and data by tenant, treat document text as untrusted, enforce authorization at tool/data access boundaries, and monitor unexpected access or egress. Confirm applicable HIPAA obligations and regional rules with counsel; ISO 27001 progress is not certification.

Centralize and protect evidence: identity-provider sign-in and role activation, GitHub reviews/checks/environment approvals and bypasses, OIDC token exchange and cloud audit trails, Pulumi/Serverless/k0s/Firebase writes, access to sensitive records, and deployment/rollback events. Correlate timestamp, actor, incident/change ID, commit, plan hash, artifact digest, partner and region; keep sensitive payloads out of logs. Send to a restricted, tamper-resistant store with role-separated access and retention matched to contracts and law; alert on missing audit feed, direct write, failed gates, unusual egress and emergency-role use. Reconcile logs to changes and periodically test that an investigator can reconstruct who proposed, reviewed, approved and executed a deployment. Define on-call rota, primary/backup, paging severity, acknowledgement/escalation times and runbooks for cross-tenant access, credential theft, data leakage and cloud outage; run tabletop exercises and post-incident reviews. Monitoring is not effective until alerts have owners and response tests.

## Limits, trade-offs and adoption order

- **Velocity vs separation:** independent approval adds latency. Fast read-only diagnosis, reusable checks, small changes and staffed on-call reduce delay; do not substitute an automated agent review for a named human. Emergency access shortens containment time through an independently approved, narrowly scoped action and carries higher audit burden.
- **Coverage gaps:** Pulumi preview may omit runtime behavior, Serverless-generated resources, Firebase configuration, drift or out-of-band cloud writes. Explicitly inventory all deploy paths and run behavioral and negative tests. Cloud administrator/root-level exceptions, compromised approvers, malicious insiders, third-party actions, upstream provider controls and unknown partner terms remain residual risks; no single GitHub gate solves them.
- **Initial priority (contain):** remove routine human/agent production write access; inventory and rotate long-lived CI credentials, replace with federated short-lived identities where supported; quarantine unreviewed MCP/plugins; protect production branches/environments; establish a named on-call and emergency procedure. Test denial paths before treating these as complete.
- **Next (make repeatable):** enforce isolated checks and protected configuration files, partner/region data classifications, reproducible artifacts and plan-bound approvals; centralize audit correlation and alert ownership; rehearse a routine change and a rollback.
- **Then (measure and expand):** close k0s/Firebase and remaining out-of-band deployment paths, add phased releases and policy-as-code coverage, partner-specific residency checks, access reviews, incident exercises and regular evidence sampling. Prioritize gaps by blast radius and evidence, not a claimed compliance badge.

## Submission hygiene: native conversation files

The challenge requires the **entire raw, unedited conversation for every coding-agent session used**, in the same GitHub repository as this deliverable. This README does not contain that transcript and is not by itself a complete submission. After this session ends, identify *all* challenge-related sessions (including resumed/compacted sessions or subagents if separately recorded) from the agent's native session directory; for Claude Code on this Windows machine, inspect `C:\Users\LEGION\.claude\projects\` for the corresponding project directory and `.jsonl` files, including any subagent session records. For other tools use their native session/export mechanism. Check timestamps, project paths and session identifiers against your challenge work so no session is omitted. Copy each native file byte-for-byte into a dedicated conversation directory under this repository without editing, truncating, redacting or reconstructing it; keep originals untouched and verify source/copy hashes and a manifest of included sessions. Session files may contain tool inputs/outputs and paths or credentials: review locally for sensitive data **before any commit or publication**. If raw files contain material you cannot safely disclose, do not publish them or silently sanitize and call them raw; seek guidance from the challenge organizers about an acceptable secure alternative. Repository submission and publication remain the candidate's decision. No cloud access, production data, deployment, commit, push or transcript publication was performed for this deliverable.

## Requirement cross-check

| Source requirement/context | Where addressed |
| --- | --- |
| Coding agent used; design DevSecOps framework despite opposing engineering/compliance needs | Scope and evidence; decision; trust boundaries; normal and emergency workflows |
| Production access from laptops, disabled permission prompts, unreviewed MCP/plugins | Trust boundaries; normal change step 2 |
| GitHub Actions long-lived token and AWS keys | CI/deployment boundary; normal change steps 4 and 6; adoption order |
| AWS, GCP, k0s, Firebase; Pulumi and Serverless; monorepo | Trust boundaries; normal change steps 3–7; limits |
| Sensitive insurer data, AI workloads and cross-country tenancy | Data, audit and operations; S3 example |
| Fragmented monitoring and informal on-call | Normal change step 7; data, audit and operations |
| ISO 27001, HIPAA and regional obligations | Scope assumptions; data, audit and operations; no unsupported compliance claim |
| Deliverables and complete, raw conversations in one GitHub repository | Submission hygiene (candidate action still outstanding) |

**Self-review:** A branch gate without cloud-side denial would leave direct production access open; the design adds cloud identity restrictions and a negative test. An environment approval without immutable revision/plan binding would permit a different change to deploy; the design requires digest and plan revalidation. A slow routine gate would delay active containment; the emergency path uses a faster independent, incident-specific human review without waiving prior approval. These are proposed checks, not proof of deployment.

Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $root -Recurse -File -Filter '*.jsonl' |

(Get-FileHash -LiteralPath $source -Algorithm SHA256).Hash -eq

content.content:
1	# DevSecOps with coding agents at Papaya
2	
3	## Scope and evidence
4	
5	**Source:** [DevSecOps Challenge 1 — DevSecOps with Coding Agents at Papaya](https://github.com/papaya-insurtech/pumpkin/blob/main/Hiring/DevSecOps_Challenges/DevSecOps_Challenge_1.md), including Appendix A. This is a proposed target operating model, not an assessment of Papaya's actual controls. I have no access to its systems, code, contracts, or production data. No control below is claimed to exist or to establish certification or legal compliance.
6	
7	**Explicit challenge requirements:** use a coding agent; design a framework and workflow for agent-assisted DevSecOps against the stated platform and opposing engineering/compliance positions; submit deliverables and *complete, raw, unedited* conversations from every agent session in one GitHub repository. The prompt leaves deliverable format open. It does not require deployment or proof of existing compliance.
8	
9	**Working assumptions to validate:** Papaya can separate production from non-production identities and isolate production deployment credentials; a central identity provider can supply named human accounts with multi-factor authentication; GitHub branch protection, environments and workload federation are available under the organization's plan; infrastructure definitions and service deployment workflows can be brought under review; each partner's residency, retention, disclosure and breach-notification requirements must be mapped with counsel and partner owners. Where a platform cannot enforce a gate, block that deployment path until an equivalent control exists rather than treating a written policy as enforcement.
10	
11	**Decision:** agents may diagnose and propose changes, but are never production approvers or holders of production write credentials. A named, independent human reviews the specific revision and production plan; a separately gated deployment identity applies only that revision. Engineering keeps a fast path to read-only diagnostics and staging. Compliance gets a technical boundary on production writes. A click alone is insufficient: authorization, artifact identity, isolation, audit and rollback must also hold.
12	
13	## Trust boundaries and enforcement
14	
15	| Boundary | Proposed enforcement | Failure behavior |
16	| --- | --- | --- |
17	| Engineer laptop and agent | Remove standing production write roles from human single sign-on profiles; provide time-limited, named, scoped read-only diagnostic access through approved access paths, with logs and sensitive-field redaction. Agent tools inherit no broader rights than the process. Put production write behind organization/account/project identity controls, not prompts, shell aliases, repository instructions or an agent's self-report. | A laptop with prompts disabled can still edit local code, but cannot mutate production. Block or expire diagnostic access if identity or device requirements fail. |
18	| Agent extensions and data | Maintain a reviewed, version-pinned allowlist for Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and plugins; assess code, dependencies, tool permissions, network destinations and update provenance in an isolated test environment. Default deny unreviewed extensions for work involving company code or data; enforce on managed endpoints and controlled runner images, not just in agent configuration. Treat partner documents, logs, issue text, repository files and tool outputs as untrusted instructions. | An unreviewed server/plugin gets no company data or credentials. A prompt-injected document cannot authorize a tool or workflow. |
19	| Source and review | Protect default and production branches: required status checks, up-to-date reviewed changes, no direct pushes, no force push or routine administrator bypass, CODEOWNERS for infrastructure/security paths, independently named human reviewer(s), and stale-review dismissal on new commits. Protect workflow, CODEOWNERS and policy files with security-owned review. Restrict bot permissions; an agent identity cannot count as a human approver. | No merge if a review, check or protected-file ownership gate fails. Audit exceptional administrative bypass separately and investigate it. |
20	| Continuous integration and deployment | Separate untrusted pull-request checks from trusted planning and deployment workflows. Run pull-request jobs with read-only repository token, no cloud secrets, and isolated runners; never run untrusted pull-request code in a privileged `pull_request_target` or equivalent context. A protected-revision planning job may obtain a separate short-lived, production **read-only** identity. A production deployment job obtains a distinct short-lived **write** identity only after its protected-environment approval. Use GitHub OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation with trust restricted to the appropriate repository, branch, workflow/environment and audience; remove long-lived repository AWS keys and GitHub personal access tokens after replacing their use. Pin third-party actions to reviewed immutable references. | A pull request cannot obtain production credentials. A write job cannot assume a role if claims, audience, repository, ref or environment do not match. |
21	| Production approval and cloud authority | Configure a protected production environment with required named reviewers and self-review prevention; only the trusted deployment workflow may request its credential. Bind deployment to the reviewed commit, immutable build artifact digest, tenant/region and plan hash. Give the deploy principal least-privilege, scoped production write permissions; deny routine human/agent write paths at the AWS organization/account and Google Cloud organization/project identity boundaries where feasible, with monitored exception roles. Restrict k0s administration and Firebase release authority to controlled deploy identities. | No direct laptop apply, missing approval or changed plan can deploy. Emergency identity is separate, short-lived, logged, independently approved before use and reviewed again afterward. |
22	
23	These gates need an adversarial test: attempt a direct laptop production write, a pull-request job credential request, an altered workflow, a self-approval, a commit pushed after approval, and a changed infrastructure plan. Each must fail at the relevant control plane. GitHub configuration alone does not stop a separately privileged cloud user; cloud identity and organization restrictions must close that route. Likewise, an OIDC role trust policy alone does not make a compromised runner harmless: keep runners ephemeral/isolated, scope roles tightly, and monitor their sessions. Configuration drift, cloud consoles, k0s credentials and Firebase release tokens are parallel write paths that must be inventoried and closed or documented as explicitly governed exceptions.
24	
25	## Normal production change: end-to-end
26	
27	1. **Request and classify.** Open a Linear change record with business owner, service, partner/country/region, data classification, intended behavior, risk, maintenance window, test and rollback owners. Check contractual residency and partner notification requirements; do not include medical records, identifiers, bank data or secrets in tickets, prompts, pull requests or build logs. Define success and abort signals before work starts.
28	2. **Develop and diagnose.** The engineer uses the coding agent against synthetic/redacted fixtures, staging, and scoped production read-only telemetry when needed. Repository and tool outputs are data, not instructions. If the agent asks to run a production write or use an unknown MCP server/plugin, stop that route; permission prompts may be off, so the cloud and network boundaries must still deny it. Record material agent-assisted changes in the pull request for reviewer context, without assuming the agent is an approver.
29	3. **Pull request.** Link the Linear record; provide architecture impact, partner/region scope, migration and backward-compatibility notes, threat considerations, test evidence, proposed infrastructure diff, rollout schedule, monitoring and rollback. Require separate human review by the relevant service owner and, for production identity, data-boundary or infrastructure changes, the security/platform owner. The author and agent cannot satisfy independent approval. Escalate high-risk cross-border or sensitive-data changes to the appropriate privacy/partner owner before deployment.
30	4. **Untrusted checks.** In isolated pull-request continuous integration, run relevant TypeScript/Node.js and Python tests, lint/type checks, migration tests, offline infrastructure validation/preview, secret scanning, dependency/container/image scanning, infrastructure-as-code policy checks and targeted security tests. Block on defined severity thresholds or require a time-bound, named exception with compensating controls; never silently waive findings. Validate Pulumi policy constraints and Serverless Framework package/configuration; test GraphQL authorization and tenancy boundaries when touched. Tests use synthetic data and no production credentials. Publish artifacts and findings with restricted visibility and redacted logs.
31	5. **Plan and independently review.** Before merge, reviewers inspect the pull-request source diff, offline preview and test evidence; approval binds to the reviewed commit. After merge, a protected-revision workflow, not pull-request code, generates the authoritative production preview using a separate short-lived, read-only planning identity for each affected scope (AWS, Google Cloud, k0s, Firebase). The preview identifies resource creates/updates/deletes, identity and data-access effects, tenant/region and cost/availability implications; a Pulumi plan alone does not cover Serverless packages or every Kubernetes/Firebase release, so attach their concrete release diffs and immutable digests too. A named independent production reviewer checks this exact plan against the merged source and request, explicitly flags destructive or cross-region changes, and approves the plan digest at the deployment gate. Limit preview access to authorized reviewers; do not put sensitive outputs in public pull-request comments. If the platform cannot produce a safe read-only production plan, use a separately reviewed equivalent and record the blind spots before approval.
32	6. **Gate and deploy.** Merge only after required pull-request checks and reviews. Build once from the protected revision, attest/store an immutable digest, and deploy that digest, not a mutable tag or a rebuilt artifact. For production, require a fresh protected-environment approval by a named human other than the initiator, **after** the authoritative plan is available. Present its digest and exact operations in the deployment run summary; capture the reviewer's named approval of that digest in a protected change record tied to the run, and make the trusted deploy job verify that record and the GitHub environment approval through authorized APIs rather than trusting an unchecked comment or a generic click. Record change ID, commit, artifact digest, approved plan digest, approver and deployment run. Before assuming its write role, the trusted workflow checks those values against the protected revision and approved artifact. Serialize conflicting changes per service/region; revalidate actual state before apply and stop for fresh independent review/approval if drift or an effective-plan change alters the approved operations. The write role is OIDC-federated only after the environment gate and is separate from the planning identity; a narrowly scoped trusted reconciliation job may use the read-only identity to check drift. If the tooling cannot apply exactly the reviewed operations, do not claim plan binding: block on any meaningful difference and require another approval. Use phased rollout/canary where supported, starting with an appropriate low-risk slice, never mixing partner datasets or regions for convenience. The pipeline, not the agent or engineer laptop, performs the production write.
33	7. **Observe and close.** Compare pre/post error rate, latency, queue depth, claim-processing accuracy, tenant-isolation signals and security/audit anomalies for a stated observation window. Assign a named primary and backup on-call owner with paging and escalation; consolidate AWS CloudWatch, Google Cloud and k0s/Firebase signals into a common incident view with tenant/region labels and traceable change IDs. Record deployment outcome and follow-up in Linear. If the threshold is exceeded, halt progression and roll back or forward-fix under the same approval rules; notify partner/privacy contacts when contractual or regulatory triggers apply.
34	
35	**Rollback is a plan, not a button.** Preserve the previous immutable service artifact and infrastructure state/preview, rehearse reversal in staging, and define who authorizes it. Reverse deployment for stateless code; for Aurora PostgreSQL schema/data changes prefer expand-contract and a tested forward repair or restore decision because rolling back code cannot reverse destructive data migrations. For S3 documents and insurer data, verify backup, retention and restoration boundaries per tenant/region. Confirm recovery-point/recovery-time objectives with service owners; do not invent guarantees. Record who triggered rollback, what changed, and whether data integrity was verified.
36	
37	### Example: production S3 claim-document access change
38	
39	A claim-service engineer proposes restricting a production S3 document bucket policy for one insurer in Vietnam. The agent helps reproduce an authorization failure against synthetic objects and drafts a Pulumi change in a pull request. The engineer includes a read-only inventory of affected principals, before/after policy diff, least-privilege access tests, expected region and partner scope, and a rollback policy version. Security and service owners independently inspect the resource preview for accidental public access, cross-tenant grants or denied legitimate claim processing; required checks pass. A named independent production approver approves the exact revision and plan. The gated pipeline assumes its short-lived AWS role, rechecks drift, applies the approved change, then observes AccessDenied rates, claim processing, audit events and S3 access patterns. If legitimate partner access breaks, the on-call owner halts rollout and restores the previously reviewed policy through the controlled path; if an active exposure requires immediate containment, use the emergency path below. A code or policy rollback does not automatically recover data already disclosed; start the incident process for that risk.
40	
41	## Emergency production change
42	
43	Example: audit signals show an insurer's claim documents may be readable by another tenant. On-call declares an incident and creates an incident/change ID; the incident commander identifies the affected region, bucket/principals and first containment action. A **named, independent human** reviews the exact emergency action, scope and expected impact and approves it before any production write; the primary or backup on-call approver is paged immediately. Prefer the pre-tested, narrowly scoped containment runbook through the gated pipeline (for example deny the suspect principal while preserving evidence); prior approval of the runbook is not a substitute for reviewing this incident's specific action. If the pipeline is unavailable, the reviewer approves an incident-bound just-in-time emergency-role activation for a different named operator, with multi-factor authentication, short expiry and the smallest write scope. Record both identities, the reviewed action and approval before activation; monitor the operator's session and compare executed commands against that scope. Never let an agent activate or approve this role. If no independent approver is reachable, escalate to the backup/incident commander; do not perform an unreviewed production write and document the resulting exposure and delay. Preserve evidence, test that access is contained without spreading sensitive data, monitor service impact, and engage security, privacy, the partner owner and legal to decide notification obligations by jurisdiction and contract. Reconcile any console/hotfix change back into Pulumi or other version-controlled desired state, revoke the emergency grant, independently review the diff and incident timeline, and rehearse recovery. Emergency access shortens the route to review; it does not waive named pre-change approval.
44	
45	## Data, audit and operations
46	
47	Maintain a per-partner/country data-flow inventory for AWS S3/Aurora, Google Cloud Vertex AI/Gemini, k0s workloads, Firebase Hosting and external model endpoints. Map where content, prompts, embeddings, logs, backups and inference are processed and retained; enforce tenant separation in identity, storage access, application authorization and tests. Decide permitted model endpoints and transfers with privacy/legal and each partner; use minimum necessary fields, redaction/tokenization, encryption in transit and at rest, access logging and retention/deletion schedules. Do not send live medical documents, national IDs, bank accounts or production secrets to an agent or third-party MCP server merely to debug faster. For production AI agents consuming uploaded documents, isolate tools and data by tenant, treat document text as untrusted, enforce authorization at tool/data access boundaries, and monitor unexpected access or egress. Confirm applicable HIPAA obligations and regional rules with counsel; ISO 27001 progress is not certification.
48

# DevSecOps with coding agents at Papaya

## Scope and evidence

**Source:** [DevSecOps Challenge 1 — DevSecOps with Coding Agents at Papaya](https://github.com/papaya-insurtech/pumpkin/blob/main/Hiring/DevSecOps_Challenges/DevSecOps_Challenge_1.md), including Appendix A. This is a proposed target operating model, not an assessment of Papaya's actual controls. I have no access to its systems, code, contracts, or production data. No control below is claimed to exist or to establish certification or legal compliance.

**Explicit challenge requirements:** use a coding agent; design a framework and workflow for agent-assisted DevSecOps against the stated platform and opposing engineering/compliance positions; submit deliverables and *complete, raw, unedited* conversations from every agent session in one GitHub repository. The prompt leaves deliverable format open. It does not require deployment or proof of existing compliance.

**Working assumptions to validate:** Papaya can separate production from non-production identities and isolate production deployment credentials; a central identity provider can supply named human accounts with multi-factor authentication; GitHub branch protection, environments and workload federation are available under the organization's plan; infrastructure definitions and service deployment workflows can be brought under review; each partner's residency, retention, disclosure and breach-notification requirements must be mapped with counsel and partner owners. Where a platform cannot enforce a gate, block that deployment path until an equivalent control exists rather than treating a written policy as enforcement.

**Decision:** agents may diagnose and propose changes, but are never production approvers or holders of production write credentials. A named, independent human reviews the specific revision and production plan; a separately gated deployment identity applies only that revision. Engineering keeps a fast path to read-only diagnostics and staging. Compliance gets a technical boundary on production writes. A click alone is insufficient: authorization, artifact identity, isolation, audit and rollback must also hold.

## Trust boundaries and enforcement

| Boundary | Proposed enforcement | Failure behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Engineer laptop and agent | Remove standing production write roles from human single sign-on profiles; provide time-limited, named, scoped read-only diagnostic access through approved access paths, with logs and sensitive-field redaction. Agent tools inherit no broader rights than the process. Put production write behind organization/account/project identity controls, not prompts, shell aliases, repository instructions or an agent's self-report. | A laptop with prompts disabled can still edit local code, but cannot mutate production. Block or expire diagnostic access if identity or device requirements fail. |
| Agent extensions and data | Maintain a reviewed, version-pinned allowlist for Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and plugins; assess code, dependencies, tool permissions, network destinations and update provenance in an isolated test environment. Default deny unreviewed extensions for work involving company code or data; enforce on managed endpoints and controlled runner images, not just in agent configuration. Treat partner documents, logs, issue text, repository files and tool outputs as untrusted instructions. | An unreviewed server/plugin gets no company data or credentials. A prompt-injected document cannot authorize a tool or workflow. |
| Source and review | Protect default and production branches: required status checks, up-to-date reviewed changes, no direct pushes, no force push or routine administrator bypass, CODEOWNERS for infrastructure/security paths, independently named human reviewer(s), and stale-review dismissal on new commits. Protect workflow, CODEOWNERS and policy files with security-owned review. Restrict bot permissions; an agent identity cannot count as a human approver. | No merge if a review, check or protected-file ownership gate fails. Audit exceptional administrative bypass separately and investigate it. |
| Continuous integration and deployment | Separate untrusted pull-request checks from trusted planning and deployment workflows. Run pull-request jobs with read-only repository token, no cloud secrets, and isolated runners; never run untrusted pull-request code in a privileged `pull_request_target` or equivalent context. A protected-revision planning job may obtain a separate short-lived, production **read-only** identity. A production deployment job obtains a distinct short-lived **write** identity only after its protected-environment approval. Use GitHub OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation with trust restricted to the appropriate repository, branch, workflow/environment and audience; remove long-lived repository AWS keys and GitHub personal access tokens after replacing their use. Pin third-party actions to reviewed immutable references. | A pull request cannot obtain production credentials. A write job cannot assume a role if claims, audience, repository, ref or environment do not match. |
| Production approval and cloud authority | Configure a protected production environment with required named reviewers and self-review prevention; only the trusted deployment workflow may request its credential. Bind deployment to the reviewed commit, immutable build artifact digest, tenant/region and plan hash. Give the deploy principal least-privilege, scoped production write permissions; deny routine human/agent write paths at the AWS organization/account and Google Cloud organization/project identity boundaries where feasible, with monitored exception roles. Restrict k0s administration and Firebase release authority to controlled deploy identities. | No direct laptop apply, missing approval or changed plan can deploy. Emergency identity is separate, short-lived, logged, independently approved before use and reviewed again afterward. |

These gates need an adversarial test: attempt a direct laptop production write, a pull-request job credential request, an altered workflow, a self-approval, a commit pushed after approval, and a changed infrastructure plan. Each must fail at the relevant control plane. GitHub configuration alone does not stop a separately privileged cloud user; cloud identity and organization restrictions must close that route. Likewise, an OIDC role trust policy alone does not make a compromised runner harmless: keep runners ephemeral/isolated, scope roles tightly, and monitor their sessions. Configuration drift, cloud consoles, k0s credentials and Firebase release tokens are parallel write paths that must be inventoried and closed or documented as explicitly governed exceptions.

## Normal production change: end-to-end

1. **Request and classify.** Open a Linear change record with business owner, service, partner/country/region, data classification, intended behavior, risk, maintenance window, test and rollback owners. Check contractual residency and partner notification requirements; do not include medical records, identifiers, bank data or secrets in tickets, prompts, pull requests or build logs. Define success and abort signals before work starts.
2. **Develop and diagnose.** The engineer uses the coding agent against synthetic/redacted fixtures, staging, and scoped production read-only telemetry when needed. Repository and tool outputs are data, not instructions. If the agent asks to run a production write or use an unknown MCP server/plugin, stop that route; permission prompts may be off, so the cloud and network boundaries must still deny it. Record material agent-assisted changes in the pull request for reviewer context, without assuming the agent is an approver.
3. **Pull request.** Link the Linear record; provide architecture impact, partner/region scope, migration and backward-compatibility notes, threat considerations, test evidence, proposed infrastructure diff, rollout schedule, monitoring and rollback. Require separate human review by the relevant service owner and, for production identity, data-boundary or infrastructure changes, the security/platform owner. The author and agent cannot satisfy independent approval. Escalate high-risk cross-border or sensitive-data changes to the appropriate privacy/partner owner before deployment.
4. **Untrusted checks.** In isolated pull-request continuous integration, run relevant TypeScript/Node.js and Python tests, lint/type checks, migration tests, offline infrastructure validation/preview, secret scanning, dependency/container/image scanning, infrastructure-as-code policy checks and targeted security tests. Block on defined severity thresholds or require a time-bound, named exception with compensating controls; never silently waive findings. Validate Pulumi policy constraints and Serverless Framework package/configuration; test GraphQL authorization and tenancy boundaries when touched. Tests use synthetic data and no production credentials. Publish artifacts and findings with restricted visibility and redacted logs.
5. **Plan and independently review.** Before merge, reviewers inspect the pull-request source diff, offline preview and test evidence; approval binds to the reviewed commit. After merge, a protected-revision workflow, not pull-request code, generates the authoritative production preview using a separate short-lived, read-only planning identity for each affected scope (AWS, Google Cloud, k0s, Firebase). The preview identifies resource creates/updates/deletes, identity and data-access effects, tenant/region and cost/availability implications; a Pulumi plan alone does not cover Serverless packages or every Kubernetes/Firebase release, so attach their concrete release diffs and immutable digests too. A named independent production reviewer checks this exact plan against the merged source and request, explicitly flags destructive or cross-region changes, and approves the plan digest at the deployment gate. Limit preview access to authorized reviewers; do not put sensitive outputs in public pull-request comments. If the platform cannot produce a safe read-only production plan, use a separately reviewed equivalent and record the blind spots before approval.
6. **Gate and deploy.** Merge only after required pull-request checks and reviews. Build once from the protected revision, attest/store an immutable digest, and deploy that digest, not a mutable tag or a rebuilt artifact. For production, require a fresh protected-environment approval by a named human other than the initiator, **after** the authoritative plan is available. Present its digest and exact operations in the deployment run summary; capture the reviewer's named approval of that digest in a protected change record tied to the run, and make the trusted deploy job verify that record and the GitHub environment approval through authorized APIs rather than trusting an unchecked comment or a generic click. Record change ID, commit, artifact digest, approved plan digest, approver and deployment run. Before assuming its write role, the trusted workflow checks those values against the protected revision and approved artifact. Serialize conflicting changes per service/region; revalidate actual state before apply and stop for fresh independent review/approval if drift or an effective-plan change alters the approved operations. The write role is OIDC-federated only after the environment gate and is separate from the planning identity; a narrowly scoped trusted reconciliation job may use the read-only identity to check drift. If the tooling cannot apply exactly the reviewed operations, do not claim plan binding: block on any meaningful difference and require another approval. Use phased rollout/canary where supported, starting with an appropriate low-risk slice, never mixing partner datasets or regions for convenience. The pipeline, not the agent or engineer laptop, performs the production write.
7. **Observe and close.** Compare pre/post error rate, latency, queue depth, claim-processing accuracy, tenant-isolation signals and security/audit anomalies for a stated observation window. Assign a named primary and backup on-call owner with paging and escalation; consolidate AWS CloudWatch, Google Cloud and k0s/Firebase signals into a common incident view with tenant/region labels and traceable change IDs. Record deployment outcome and follow-up in Linear. If the threshold is exceeded, halt progression and roll back or forward-fix under the same approval rules; notify partner/privacy contacts when contractual or regulatory triggers apply.

**Rollback is a plan, not a button.** Preserve the previous immutable service artifact and infrastructure state/preview, rehearse reversal in staging, and define who authorizes it. Reverse deployment for stateless code; for Aurora PostgreSQL schema/data changes prefer expand-contract and a tested forward repair or restore decision because rolling back code cannot reverse destructive data migrations. For S3 documents and insurer data, verify backup, retention and restoration boundaries per tenant/region. Confirm recovery-point/recovery-time objectives with service owners; do not invent guarantees. Record who triggered rollback, what changed, and whether data integrity was verified.

### Example: production S3 claim-document access change

A claim-service engineer proposes restricting a production S3 document bucket policy for one insurer in Vietnam. The agent helps reproduce an authorization failure against synthetic objects and drafts a Pulumi change in a pull request. The engineer includes a read-only inventory of affected principals, before/after policy diff, least-privilege access tests, expected region and partner scope, and a rollback policy version. Security and service owners independently inspect the resource preview for accidental public access, cross-tenant grants or denied legitimate claim processing; required checks pass. A named independent production approver approves the exact revision and plan. The gated pipeline assumes its short-lived AWS role, rechecks drift, applies the approved change, then observes AccessDenied rates, claim processing, audit events and S3 access patterns. If legitimate partner access breaks, the on-call owner halts rollout and restores the previously reviewed policy through the controlled path; if an active exposure requires immediate containment, use the emergency path below. A code or policy rollback does not automatically recover data already disclosed; start the incident process for that risk.

## Emergency production change

Example: audit signals show an insurer's claim documents may be readable by another tenant. On-call declares an incident and creates an incident/change ID; the incident commander identifies the affected region, bucket/principals and first containment action. A **named, independent human** reviews the exact emergency action, scope and expected impact and approves it before any production write; the primary or backup on-call approver is paged immediately. Prefer the pre-tested, narrowly scoped containment runbook through the gated pipeline (for example deny the suspect principal while preserving evidence); prior approval of the runbook is not a substitute for reviewing this incident's specific action. If the pipeline is unavailable, the reviewer approves an incident-bound just-in-time emergency-role activation for a different named operator, with multi-factor authentication, short expiry and the smallest write scope. Record both identities, the reviewed action and approval before activation; monitor the operator's session and compare executed commands against that scope. Never let an agent activate or approve this role. If no independent approver is reachable, escalate to the backup/incident commander; do not perform an unreviewed production write and document the resulting exposure and delay. Preserve evidence, test that access is contained without spreading sensitive data, monitor service impact, and engage security, privacy, the partner owner and legal to decide notification obligations by jurisdiction and contract. Reconcile any console/hotfix change back into Pulumi or other version-controlled desired state, revoke the emergency grant, independently review the diff and incident timeline, and rehearse recovery. Emergency access shortens the route to review; it does not waive named pre-change approval.

## Data, audit and operations

Maintain a per-partner/country data-flow inventory for AWS S3/Aurora, Google Cloud Vertex AI/Gemini, k0s workloads, Firebase Hosting and external model endpoints. Map where content, prompts, embeddings, logs, backups and inference are processed and retained; enforce tenant separation in identity, storage access, application authorization and tests. Decide permitted model endpoints and transfers with privacy/legal and each partner; use minimum necessary fields, redaction/tokenization, encryption in transit and at rest, access logging and retention/deletion schedules. Do not send live medical documents, national IDs, bank accounts or production secrets to an agent or third-party MCP server merely to debug faster. For production AI agents consuming uploaded documents, isolate tools and data by tenant, treat document text as untrusted, enforce authorization at tool/data access boundaries, and monitor unexpected access or egress. Confirm applicable HIPAA obligations and regional rules with counsel; ISO 27001 progress is not certification.

Centralize and protect evidence: identity-provider sign-in and role activation, GitHub reviews/checks/environment approvals and bypasses, OIDC token exchange and cloud audit trails, Pulumi/Serverless/k0s/Firebase writes, access to sensitive records, and deployment/rollback events. Correlate timestamp, actor, incident/change ID, commit, plan hash, artifact digest, partner and region; keep sensitive payloads out of logs. Send to a restricted, tamper-resistant store with role-separated access and retention matched to contracts and law; alert on missing audit feed, direct write, failed gates, unusual egress and emergency-role use. Reconcile logs to changes and periodically test that an investigator can reconstruct who proposed, reviewed, approved and executed a deployment. Define on-call rota, primary/backup, paging severity, acknowledgement/escalation times and runbooks for cross-tenant access, credential theft, data leakage and cloud outage; run tabletop exercises and post-incident reviews. Monitoring is not effective until alerts have owners and response tests.

## Limits, trade-offs and adoption order

- **Velocity vs separation:** independent approval adds latency. Fast read-only diagnosis, reusable checks, small changes and staffed on-call reduce delay; do not substitute an automated agent review for a named human. Emergency access shortens containment time through an independently approved, narrowly scoped action and carries higher audit burden.
- **Coverage gaps:** Pulumi preview may omit runtime behavior, Serverless-generated resources, Firebase configuration, drift or out-of-band cloud writes. Explicitly inventory all deploy paths and run behavioral and negative tests. Cloud administrator/root-level exceptions, compromised approvers, malicious insiders, third-party actions, upstream provider controls and unknown partner terms remain residual risks; no single GitHub gate solves them.
- **Initial priority (contain):** remove routine human/agent production write access; inventory and rotate long-lived CI credentials, replace with federated short-lived identities where supported; quarantine unreviewed MCP/plugins; protect production branches/environments; establish a named on-call and emergency procedure. Test denial paths before treating these as complete.
- **Next (make repeatable):** enforce isolated checks and protected configuration files, partner/region data classifications, reproducible artifacts and plan-bound approvals; centralize audit correlation and alert ownership; rehearse a routine change and a rollback.
- **Then (measure and expand):** close k0s/Firebase and remaining out-of-band deployment paths, add phased releases and policy-as-code coverage, partner-specific residency checks, access reviews, incident exercises and regular evidence sampling. Prioritize gaps by blast radius and evidence, not a claimed compliance badge.

## Submission hygiene: native conversation files

The challenge requires the **entire raw, unedited conversation for every coding-agent session used**, in the same GitHub repository as this deliverable. This README does not contain that transcript and is not by itself a complete submission. After this session ends, identify *all* challenge-related sessions, including resumed sessions and separately stored subagent records. For Claude Code on Windows, inspect the workspace's directory under `$HOME\.claude\projects\` and its `.jsonl` files; for other agents, use their native session/export location. Do not rely on a summary or this README as the conversation. Compare timestamps, session identifiers and challenge-related content locally; a single session may include unrelated work, so review the **entire** file for disclosure risk. For a local PowerShell example (run only after the session has closed):

```powershell
$root = Join-Path $HOME '.claude\projects'
Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $root -Recurse -File -Filter '*.jsonl' |
  Where-Object { $_.FullName -match 'Claude-Workspace' } |
  Select-Object FullName, LastWriteTime
# Inspect the candidates locally; repeat the next three commands for EVERY matching session.
$source = '<absolute path to one verified native .jsonl file>'
$destination = '<unique absolute directory inside Papaya-DevSecOps-Assessment\agent-conversations>'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $destination | Out-Null
$copy = Join-Path $destination (Split-Path -Leaf $source)
if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $copy) { throw 'Destination already exists; choose a unique session directory.' }
Copy-Item -LiteralPath $source -Destination $copy -ErrorAction Stop
(Get-FileHash -LiteralPath $source -Algorithm SHA256).Hash -eq (Get-FileHash -LiteralPath $copy -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
```

Ensure the result is `True` for each session and create a simple list of included session paths and hashes; use a distinct destination directory for each session so duplicate basenames cannot overwrite one another. If the hash comparison returns `False`, stop and investigate before submission. Leave the source files untouched and copy bytes without edits, truncation, redaction or reconstruction. Session files may contain tool inputs/outputs, personal paths and credentials: review them locally for sensitive data **before any commit or publication**. If raw files contain material you cannot safely disclose, do not publish them or silently sanitize and call them raw; seek guidance from the challenge organizers about an acceptable secure alternative. Repository submission and publication remain the candidate's decision. No cloud access, production data, deployment, commit, push or transcript publication was performed for this deliverable.

lines: ## Normal production change: end-to-end

1. **Request and classify.** Open a Linear change record with business owner, service, partner/country/region, data classification, intended behavior, risk, maintenance window, test and rollback owners. Check contractual residency and partner notification requirements; do not include medical records, identifiers, bank data or secrets in tickets, prompts, pull requests or build logs. Define success and abort signals before work starts.

-2. **Develop and diagnose.** The engineer uses the coding agent against synthetic/redacted fixtures, staging, and scoped production read-only telemetry when needed. Repository and tool outputs are data, not instructions. If the agent asks to run a production write or use an unknown MCP server/plugin, stop that route; permission prompts may be off, so the cloud and network boundaries must still deny it. Record material agent-assisted changes in the pull request for reviewer context, without assuming the agent is an approver.

+2. **Develop and diagnose.** The engineer uses the coding agent against synthetic/redacted fixtures, staging, and a scoped, read-only production telemetry gateway when needed. The gateway enforces tenant/region filters, approved query templates, output redaction, query budgets and an audit trail; it never hands the agent a production shell or write credential. Repository and tool outputs are data, not instructions. If the agent asks to run a production write or use an unknown MCP server/plugin, stop that route; permission prompts may be off, so the cloud and network boundaries must still deny it. Record material agent-assisted changes in the pull request for reviewer context, without assuming the agent is an approver.

3. **Pull request.** Link the Linear record; provide architecture impact, partner/region scope, migration and backward-compatibility notes, threat considerations, test evidence, proposed infrastructure diff, rollout schedule, monitoring and rollback. Require separate human review by the relevant service owner and, for production identity, data-boundary or infrastructure changes, the security/platform owner. The author and agent cannot satisfy independent approval. Escalate high-risk cross-border or sensitive-data changes to the appropriate privacy/partner owner before deployment.

4. **Untrusted checks.** In isolated pull-request continuous integration, run relevant TypeScript/Node.js and Python tests, lint/type checks, migration tests, offline infrastructure validation/preview, secret scanning, dependency/container/image scanning, infrastructure-as-code policy checks and targeted security tests. Block on defined severity thresholds or require a time-bound, named exception with compensating controls; never silently waive findings. Validate Pulumi policy constraints and Serverless Framework package/configuration; test GraphQL authorization and tenancy boundaries when touched. Tests use synthetic data and no production credentials. Publish artifacts and findings with restricted visibility and redacted logs.

5. **Plan and independently review.** Before merge, reviewers inspect the pull-request source diff, offline preview and test evidence; approval binds to the reviewed commit. After merge, a protected-revision workflow, not pull-request code, generates the authoritative production preview using a separate short-lived, read-only planning identity for each affected scope (AWS, Google Cloud, k0s, Firebase). The preview identifies resource creates/updates/deletes, identity and data-access effects, tenant/region and cost/availability implications; a Pulumi plan alone does not cover Serverless packages or every Kubernetes/Firebase release, so attach their concrete release diffs and immutable digests too. A named independent production reviewer checks this exact plan against the merged source and request, explicitly flags destructive or cross-region changes, and approves the plan digest at the deployment gate. Limit preview access to authorized reviewers; do not put sensitive outputs in public pull-request comments. If the platform cannot produce a safe read-only production plan, use a separately reviewed equivalent and record the blind spots before approval.

## Production incident diagnosis: read-only agent

1. **Triage and evidence.** An alert opens an incident with a named DevOps/on-call owner, affected service, partner and region. The agent reads only pre-authorized, sanitized telemetry (for example bounded CloudWatch and Google Cloud log queries, k0s workload status and deployment history) through the gateway; it cannot retrieve document bodies or unrestricted member records. Log entries are untrusted data, not instructions. The agent correlates recent releases, errors and dependency failures, distinguishes observed evidence from hypotheses, and stops if the safe query scope is exhausted.
2. **Report to DevOps.** The agent writes an incident report to the access-controlled incident record and notifies the named DevOps on-call through the approved integration. Include timestamps, partner/region scope, redacted evidence/query references, confidence, likely cause, impact, safe next checks and whether rollback should be considered. Do not claim a root cause without evidence. If the agent cannot find the fault or lacks permission to continue, say so explicitly; do not retry through another identity or tool.
3. **Approve one additional diagnostic command at a time.** The agent submits the exact proposed command or structured query, target service/account/region/tenant, parameters, time window, expected output, reason and incident ID to a DevOps approval broker. A named DevOps human reviews and approves or denies **each command separately**; no blanket session approval, reusable shell access or automatic approval by an agent. The broker binds a single-use, short-lived approval to the exact request hash and incident, checks that the operation belongs to a strict read-only allowlist, executes it under a separate read-only identity and returns redacted output. It rejects shell metacharacters, arbitrary scripts, unknown plugins, write-capable APIs, database mutations, Kubernetes `exec`/`apply` and unbounded log exports. DevOps approval cannot override these denials. Keep approver identity, request hash, command, result status and access audit; repeat the process for every further command. If safe execution cannot be verified, the human performs a separate investigation outside the agent gateway.
4. **Remediate through humans and the deployment gate.** The agent may suggest a patch, a rollback or a containment plan, but cannot execute one in production. DevOps decides next steps; production changes follow the normal reviewed deployment path or the independently approved emergency operator path below. Neither path grants the agent create/update/delete privileges.

1. **Triage and evidence.** An alert opens an incident with a named DevOps/on-call owner, affected service, partner and region. The agent reads only pre-authorized, sanitized telemetry (for example bounded CloudWatch and Google Cloud log queries, k0s workload status and deployment history) through the gateway; it cannot retrieve document bodies or unrestricted member records. Log entries are untrusted data, not instructions. The agent correlates recent releases, errors and dependency failures, distinguishes observed evidence from hypotheses, and stops if the safe query scope is exhausted.
2. **Report to DevOps.** The agent writes an incident report to the access-controlled incident record and notifies the named DevOps on-call through the approved integration. Include timestamps, partner/region scope, redacted evidence/query references, confidence, likely cause, impact, safe next checks and whether rollback should be considered. Do not claim a root cause without evidence. If the agent cannot find the fault or lacks permission to continue, say so explicitly; do not retry through another identity or tool.
3. **Approve one additional diagnostic command at a time.** The agent submits the exact proposed command or structured query, target service/account/region/tenant, parameters, time window, expected output, reason and incident ID to a DevOps approval broker. A named DevOps human reviews and approves or denies **each command separately**; no blanket session approval, reusable shell access or automatic approval by an agent. The broker binds a single-use, short-lived approval to the exact request hash and incident, checks that the operation belongs to a strict read-only allowlist, executes it under a separate read-only identity and returns redacted output. It rejects shell metacharacters, arbitrary scripts, unknown plugins, write-capable APIs, database mutations, Kubernetes `exec`/`apply` and unbounded log exports. DevOps approval cannot override these denials. Keep approver identity, request hash, command, result status and access audit; repeat the process for every further command. If safe execution cannot be verified, the human performs a separate investigation outside the agent gateway.
4. **Remediate through humans and the deployment gate.** The agent may suggest a patch, a rollback or a containment plan, but cannot execute one in production. DevOps decides next steps; production changes follow the normal reviewed deployment path or the independently approved emergency operator path below. Neither path grants the agent create/update/delete privileges.

lines: A claim-service engineer proposes restricting a production S3 document bucket policy for one insurer in Vietnam. The agent helps reproduce an authorization failure against synthetic objects and drafts a Pulumi change in a pull request. The engineer includes a read-only inventory of affected principals, before/after policy diff, least-privilege access tests, expected region and partner scope, and a rollback policy version. Security and service owners independently inspect the resource preview for accidental public access, cross-tenant grants or denied legitimate claim processing; required checks pass. A named independent production approver approves the exact revision and plan. The gated pipeline assumes its short-lived AWS role, rechecks drift, applies the approved change, then observes AccessDenied rates, claim processing, audit events and S3 access patterns. If legitimate partner access breaks, the on-call owner halts rollout and restores the previously reviewed policy through the controlled path; if an active exposure requires immediate containment, use the emergency path below. A code or policy rollback does not automatically recover data already disclosed; start the incident process for that risk.

## Emergency production change

Example: audit signals show an insurer's claim documents may be readable by another tenant. On-call declares an incident and creates an incident/change ID; the incident commander identifies the affected region, bucket/principals and first containment action. A **named, independent human** reviews the exact emergency action, scope and expected impact and approves it before any production write; the primary or backup on-call approver is paged immediately. Prefer the pre-tested, narrowly scoped containment runbook through the gated pipeline (for example deny the suspect principal while preserving evidence); prior approval of the runbook is not a substitute for reviewing this incident's specific action. If the pipeline is unavailable, the reviewer approves an incident-bound just-in-time emergency-role activation for a different named operator, with multi-factor authentication, short expiry and the smallest write scope. Record both identities, the reviewed action and approval before activation; monitor the operator's session and compare executed commands against that scope. Never let an agent activate or approve this role. If no independent approver is reachable, escalate to the backup/incident commander; do not perform an unreviewed production write and document the resulting exposure and delay. Preserve evidence, test that access is contained without spreading sensitive data, monitor service impact, and engage security, privacy, the partner owner and legal to decide notification obligations by jurisdiction and contract. Reconcile any console/hotfix change back into Pulumi or other version-controlled desired state, revoke the emergency grant, independently review the diff and incident timeline, and rehearse recovery. Emergency access shortens the route to review; it does not waive named pre-change approval.

Assign a named primary and backup on-call owner with paging and escalation; consolidate AWS CloudWatch, Google Cloud and k0s/Firebase signals into a common incident view with tenant/region labels and traceable change IDs.
